title: "file.txt:hidden" isn't a second file on NTFS — it's extra data bolted onto file.txt that `dir` will never show you
assumption: A colon in a filename is just another character, and a name containing one refers to a distinct file.

input.description: A filename accepted from user input (or produced by careless string concatenation) that is later written to an actual NTFS volume.

what_goes_wrong: On NTFS, writing to "file.txt:hidden" doesn't create a new file — it creates (or overwrites) an alternate data stream attached to the EXISTING file.txt, invisible to a normal directory listing and not counted in the visible file's reported size, so arbitrary extra data can be smuggled in behind an ordinary-looking file.
why: NTFS filenames support multiple named 'data streams' per file entry, addressed as "name:stream"; the unnamed stream is the file's normal content, and "file.txt:hidden" addresses an additional stream on the SAME directory entry as file.txt, not a sibling file. Pure path libraries have no awareness of this NTFS-specific syntax at all — they just see a colon character — so splitext and basename don't special-case it; splitext even folds the whole ":hidden" suffix into what it reports as the file's 'extension'.
affects: python ntpath (no ads awareness — colon is just a character)

repros.code:
import ntpath
name = "file.txt:hidden"
print("splitdrive:", ntpath.splitdrive(name))
print("splitext:", ntpath.splitext(name))
print("basename:", ntpath.basename(name))

fix: Reject colons in filenames outright before they reach a Windows filesystem unless you specifically intend to address a named stream, and never rely on directory listings or visible file size alone to audit what's actually stored in a file.

sources.title: Microsoft Sysinternals: Streams (NTFS Alternate Data Streams)
Microsoft Learn: Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces

test_cases.note: Your filename validator should reject or specifically handle a colon before it reaches a Windows filesystem call.
